findings.paper_title: Write-off of irrecoverable debt over £50,000
findings.headline: Poundland and River Island subject to high court restructuring plans; Norwich unable to recover £320,587.04 in business rates debt
findings.detail: River Island Clothing Company Ltd and Poundland Ltd are subject to part 26A restructuring plans sanctioned by the High Court (08/08/2025 and 26/08/2025 respectively). The council is owed £157,250.00 from River Island and £163,337.04 from Poundland. After exhausting all debt recovery procedures, the council is writing off both debts as irrecoverable and does not expect dividend recovery.
findings.matters: Two significant commercial occupiers entering restructuring indicates commercial property market stress in Norwich and demonstrates credit risk concentration among major business ratepayers
findings.figures: River Island £157,250.00, Poundland £163,337.04, total £320,587.04
findings.quote: It is unlikely we will receive any dividend in these cases, but should any dividend be received in the future the write-off can be reversed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Auditor’s Annual Report for Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Council's audit recovery remains significantly behind expected timescale; 2025/26 opinion likely to be disclaimed, unqualified opinion unlikely before 2027/28
findings.detail: EY notes the council is behind the timeline set out in the NAO's Local Audit Reset and Recovery Implementation Guidance. Unable to complete procedures in both 2023/24 and 2024/25 due to weaknesses in council arrangements. The 2025/26 audit opinion will likely also be disclaimed due to pervasive gaps in assurance over opening balances and comparators. Recovery to an unqualified opinion is unlikely and may depend on achieving Property, Plant & Equipment revaluations not yet completed.
findings.matters: Multi-year disclaimer opinions prevent reliable financial reporting. Lenders cannot assess the council's true financial health when financial statements lack audit assurance for multiple years.
findings.figures: 2023/24 (disclaimed), 2024/25 (disclaimed), 2025/26 (likely disclaimed), 2026/27+ (possibly qualified)
findings.quote: The Council is currently behind the illustrative timescale for the process of re-building assurance, because not all audit procedures were completed during either 2023/24 or 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Auditor’s Annual Report for Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Non-compliance with laws and regulations not reported to auditors for seven months; council lacks formal whistleblowing logs and weak investigation processes
findings.detail: EY identified one instance of non-compliance. Investigation began internally in October 2024, but auditors were not informed until May 2025 — a seven-month delay. The council was slow to recognise the significance of the matter. Key roles (S151 Officer and Monitoring Officer) were new in post when the matter emerged. The council lacks formal whistleblowing logs. Some investigation elements were only considered following auditor challenge.
findings.matters: Weak non-compliance procedures, slow reporting, and lack of whistleblowing mechanisms suggest governance and control environment deficiencies. Seven-month delays increase reputational and legal risk.
findings.figures: October 2024 (investigation started), May 2025 (auditors informed)
findings.quote: Officers did not inform us of the matter in a timely fashion. Actions were taken internally to investigate the matter from October 2024, however, EY were not informed until May 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Auditor’s Annual Report for Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Key working papers not provided on time or in proper format; inadequate supporting evidence for property valuations and other accounting estimates
findings.detail: A number of key working papers were not provided in accordance with agreed timetables or suitable formats for audit sampling. The most significant issues were with creditors, debtors, property plant & equipment, other income and expenditure, and Housing Revenue Account. Creditors and debtors working papers included significant opening and gross balances that did not meet audit specifications. Insufficient input data was provided for land and building valuations, affecting auditors' ability to complete procedures. Management acknowledged further work is required.
findings.matters: Weak audit working papers and delayed evidence suggest the finance team lacks capacity or capability to support financial reporting, increasing audit risk and delaying audit sign-off.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: The creditors and debtors working papers did not meet the requirements set out in our working paper request, as they included significant opening and gross balances.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Auditor’s Annual Report for Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Financial statements published 26 September 2025, missing the 30 June deadline by three months, due to delays finalising group accounts
findings.detail: The council failed to meet the 30 June 2025 regulatory deadline under the Accounts and Audit Regulations. A Notice of Delay was issued, and statements were subsequently published on 26 September 2025. The delay was attributed to difficulties finalising the group financial statements, including issues with consolidation of the subsidiary accounts.
findings.matters: Financial reporting delays indicate capacity or competence issues in the finance team and increase the period during which errors could go undetected. Three-month delays in statutory reporting are unusual.
findings.figures: 30 June 2025 (deadline), 26 September 2025 (actual publication)
findings.quote: The financial statements were not published by the 30 June 2025 deadline set out in the Accounts and Audit Regulations. This was due to delays in finalising the group financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Auditor’s Annual Report for Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Pension liability in 2023/24 was overstated by £35.1 million due to missing asset ceiling adjustment
findings.detail: In 2023/24, the council did not request an asset ceiling adjustment from the pension fund actuary. This resulted in the defined pension liability being overstated by £35.1 million. The actuary later identified this misstatement through an updated asset ceiling report, but no adjustment was made to the financial statements which received a disclaimer opinion.
findings.matters: A £35.1m overstatement is material and significantly affects the council's reported liabilities, reserves and financial position reported to creditors and lenders.
findings.figures: £35.1 million
findings.quote: the Council did not request an asset ceiling adjustment, therefore the balances in the financial statements (upon which we disclaimed our audit opinion) contained a material misstatement. Consequently, management obtained an updated asset ceiling report from the actuary highlighting that the defined pension liability was overstated by £35.1 million.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Auditor’s Annual Report for Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Council lacked effective governance frameworks for subsidiaries, allowing Lion Homes to operate independently with no requirement to report issues to the Council
findings.detail: The council had no adequate policies or procedures for oversight of its subsidiaries. Lion Homes was established with Articles of Association providing minimal Council interaction. There was no mandatory requirement for the subsidiary to report to the Council; subsidiary directors had discretion whether to report issues. The Shareholder Panel terms of reference were minimal, with no guidance on reporting, governance or decision-making. Constitution review showed not all subsidiaries were even referenced.
findings.matters: This significant governance weakness means the council lacks control over its assets and liabilities. Similar oversights could affect other council entities, exposing the council to unmonitored financial risk.
findings.figures: 2015 (year incorporated); July 2025 (liquidation decision)
findings.quote: Where issues have been experienced, the directors of the subsidiary had the power to report issues to the Council at their discretion and, since there were no established policies, there was no breach of procedure if they chose not to do so.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Auditor’s Annual Report for Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Council's wholly-owned subsidiary Lion Homes Limited entered member voluntary liquidation after material errors and loss of viability
findings.detail: EY identified increased risk to the financial sustainability of Lion Homes Limited, incorporated in 2015 as a housing company. Material errors were identified in the subsidiary's draft financial statements consolidated into 2023/24. Following external review in October 2024 identifying significant financial risk, the company paused activity. Cabinet approved member voluntary liquidation in July 2025.
findings.matters: Shows the council's inability to effectively oversee its trading entities, resulted in accumulated losses and required bailout/liquidation, exposing taxpayers and creditors to financial loss.
findings.figures: July 2025 (liquidation approved), October 2024 (financial review commissioned)
findings.quote: During the 2024/25 statutory audit we were made aware of increased risk concerning the financial sustainability of Lion Homes Limited, a subsidiary company of the Council. Management are considering the options for the future of the company.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Auditor’s Annual Report for Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: EY issued a disclaimer of opinion on 2024/25 financial statements, unable to obtain sufficient evidence over balances and movements
findings.detail: EY disclaimed its opinion on 23 March 2026, stating it had not obtained sufficient evidence to have reasonable assurance over all in-year movements and closing balances. This cascades from the 2023/24 disclaimer, meaning opening balances and comparators lack assurance. The lack of evidence means EY could not conclude the statements are free from material and pervasive misstatement.
findings.matters: A disclaimer is the most serious audit outcome. Financial statements cannot be relied upon by lenders assessing the council's true financial position and creditworthiness.
findings.figures: 23 March 2026 (disclaimer issued)
findings.quote: Although the level of assurance gained has increased, we have not yet obtained sufficient evidence to have reasonable assurance over all in-year movements and closing balances.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Budget Outturn Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: Budget Risk Reserve drawn down £2.8m in single year to £4.3m, flagging emerging cost pressures
findings.detail: General Fund Budget Risk Reserve reduced from £6.6m opening to £4.3m closing by drawing £2.8m in 2025-26 to cover one-off projects (£129k for Local Government Reorganisation prep, £1.5m to Lion Homes Reserve for member voluntary liquidation and doubtful debts, £500k to new Feasibility Reserve). While reserve remains above zero, scale of drawdown suggests underlying financial pressures.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion at this rate is unsustainable; if pattern continues, council exhausts discretionary reserves within few years, reducing financial flexibility for unexpected costs or demand spikes.
findings.quote: £2,845,000 of the Budget Risk Reserve has been utilised in the year to support one-off projects, with £129,000 supporting costs arising from preparations for Local Government Reorganisation...£1,500,000 was transferred to the Lion Homes Reserve and £500,000 to the Feasibility Reserve

findings.paper_title: Provisional Budget Outturn Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: Anglia Square demolition project delayed with £16.8m underspend due to scope increase discovered mid-project
findings.detail: Anglia Square project (£16.8m of total £22.3m General Fund capital underspend) is significantly behind schedule. Additional survey work after tenant vacation revealed further strip-out work required than originally planned. Completion now 2026-27; Homes England approved grant extension but scope increase represents delivery and cost risk.
findings.matters: Largest single capital underspend driven by delayed delivery and mid-project scope expansion; indicates project estimation and management challenges; further unforeseen costs could emerge during execution.
findings.figures: £16,767,000 underspent in 2025-26; project extends into 2026-27
findings.quote: Additional survey work once tenants had vacated showed further strip out work was required. This delayed the project, but the demolition programme will complete in 2026-2027 and grant extension approved by Homes England

findings.paper_title: Provisional Budget Outturn Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: Water charges pass-through requirement created £2m annual cost obligation on HRA
findings.detail: Arrangement with Anglian Water includes requirement to pass commission received on water charges to tenants. Generated £2 million HRA cost in 2025-26, mitigated by drawing on HRA reserves set aside for this purpose. Payments applied to tenants' rent accounts.
findings.matters: Material new recurring cost obligation arising from water company arrangement; represents significant ongoing liability on HRA finances with limited council control.
findings.figures: £2,000,000 in 2025-26 requirement
findings.quote: The requirement to make payments to tenants in respect commission received for the collection of water charges, generated additional costs of £2,000,000 in the year, although some of this has been mitigated by utilising a provision included within the HRA prudent minimum reserve balance

findings.paper_title: Provisional Budget Outturn Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: Homelessness costs are entirely grant-dependent with housing benefit component exceeding current caps by £601k
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation and housing benefit costs were offset by £1.044m grant income, but the paper specifically identifies housing benefit costs for short-term accommodation that are 'above the current cap' at £601,000. Cost structure relies on grant income plus reserve drawdown; if funding changes, council faces direct shortfall.
findings.matters: Homelessness costs exceed government housing benefit caps; council funding gap is grant-dependent and not sustainable if grant income ceases or reduces.
findings.figures: £1,044,000 grant income offsetting £455,000 temp accommodation plus £601,000 above-cap housing benefit
findings.quote: Additional grant income (£1,044,000) has offset the additional costs of temporary accommodation (£455,000) and the cost of housing benefit for short-term accommodation above the current cap (£601,000)

findings.paper_title: Provisional Budget Outturn Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: Planning application income fell £461k short due to Nutrient Neutrality impacts on development industry
findings.detail: External regulatory uncertainty around Nutrient Neutrality continues to depress development activity and planning applications. Generated £461,000 income shortfall against budget in 2025-26, reducing net General Fund position.
findings.matters: Planning fees are volatile and driven by external regulatory factors beyond council control; timing of regulatory clarity remains uncertain, creating forward-looking income uncertainty.
findings.figures: £461,000 shortfall against budgeted planning income
findings.quote: income from planning applications has been £461,000 lower than budgeted as the development industry has continued to be impacted by uncertainties linked to Nutrient Neutrality

findings.paper_title: Provisional Budget Outturn Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: NCSL job evaluation created £530k+ recurring cost pressure on General Fund, plus significant HRA impacts
findings.detail: The council instructed Norwich City Services Ltd to align pay on building and environmental contracts with council pay-scales. Although NCSL funded the evaluation, resulting pay increases fall to the council as sole shareholder. Generated £530,000 General Fund cost, plus £466,000 HRA building contract costs and £443,000 environmental services costs in 2025-26.
findings.matters: This is a new permanent recurring cost from the council's wholly-owned company, materializing as a structural budget pressure rather than one-off.
findings.figures: £530,000 General Fund; £466,000 HRA building contract; £443,000 HRA environmental
findings.quote: the council instructed its wholly owned company, Norwich City Services Ltd (NCSL) to implement a full job evaluation exercise to bring pay across both the building and environmental contracts, into line with council pay-scales...has generated additional costs of £530,000 to the General Fund in the year

findings.paper_title: Regulator of Social Housing Regulatory Judgement
findings.headline: HRA funding will be focused on delivering Regulator improvement plans, potentially reshaping HRA priorities for 2026-27
findings.detail: The council states 'This may mean we focus HRA resources on achieving these plans this financial year' and that changes to HRA funding focus will be made 'in conjunction with the Council's S.151 Officer.' This indicates HRA budget flexibility or potential reallocation to meet regulatory requirements.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know whether HRA spending is being redirected away from other service areas or reserves to meet regulatory compliance. This affects HRA financial forecasts and borrowing headroom.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: The C1 rating and report from the Regulator means we can continue with existing improvement plans. However, the Regulator expects to see improvement plans being delivered. This may mean we focus HRA resources on achieving these plans this financial year.

findings.paper_title: Regulator of Social Housing Regulatory Judgement
findings.headline: Stock condition survey must reach 100% coverage by December 2026; currently at 80%
findings.detail: The Regulator required completion of physical stock condition surveys on all council homes by end-2026. The council started the year at 80% coverage. Failure to complete will breach a specific Regulator expectation and may trigger compliance concerns.
findings.matters: Incomplete stock surveys limit the council's understanding of future maintenance/repair liabilities and capital planning. This could lead to unexpected HRA spending or underestimation of long-term asset condition.
findings.figures: Current coverage: 80%. Required by December 2026: 100%
findings.quote: Whilst the Regulator noted the good property data Norwich held and progress with Stock Condition Surveys, they wanted to see us complete the journey to 100% stock condition coverage by December 2026. This means a physical stock condition survey of all our council homes by the end of this year. We started the year with 80% coverage.

findings.paper_title: Regulator of Social Housing Regulatory Judgement
findings.headline: Resource constraints and rising tenant demand pose delivery risk for entire improvement programme
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies risk from 'increasing customer demand and the demands on colleague resources' as potentially preventing delivery of the improvement plans. The Better Homes Board oversees all improvement delivery, but staffing/capacity is a named constraint.
findings.matters: Resource pressure could force HRA spending increases (recruitment, agency staffing, contractor costs) to meet regulatory requirements, or lead to non-delivery and regulatory action.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: The risk is we are unable to deliver due increasing customer demand and the demands on colleague resources.

findings.paper_title: Regulator of Social Housing Regulatory Judgement
findings.headline: Repairs service significantly behind 2026-27 target, with 60-day current cycle versus 30-day target
findings.detail: The Regulator noted repairs 'was described as the service area where the grading could have been lower than a C1.' Current non-emergency repair timescale is 60 days; the council has committed to a 30-day target for 2026-27. The council must show continued improvement in completion times and backlog reduction.
findings.matters: A 60-day repairs cycle indicates either operational inefficiency, resource shortfall, or contractor capacity issues—each carrying HRA cost implications. Failure to meet the 30-day commitment risks regulatory downgrade and higher tenant complaint/ombudsman costs.
findings.figures: Current non-emergency repairs timescale: 60 days. 2026-27 target: 30 days
findings.quote: RSH acknowledged that: The current non-emergency repairs timescale of 60 days is high. [noting that the council and NCSL have agreed a 30-day target for this year, 2026-2027]

findings.paper_title: Regulator of Social Housing Regulatory Judgement
findings.headline: Medium risk of regulatory downgrade if improvement plans are not delivered within the next year
findings.detail: The council identified medium risk that it could be downgraded from C1 if it fails to meet the Regulator's improvement plan commitments. The risk explicitly states there is 'significant work in a short period needed to stay on track.' The Regulator will revisit progress at annual engagement meetings.
findings.matters: A regulatory downgrade would signal weakness in HRA management and could affect the council's borrowing capacity and terms. It would also require formal remedial action plans.
findings.figures: C1 grade currently held by only 54 housing providers nationally as of April 2026, with just 9 being local authorities
findings.quote: The risks posed by the current situation is that Norwich is unable to deliver its improvement plans meaning a downgraded C rating in the Consumer Standards. This is currently medium risk as we have good and clear plans in place, but there is significant work in a short period needed to stay on track.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement, 2025-26
findings.headline: Balanced budget achieved for 2026/27 without drawing reserves, but significant capital underspends suggest delivery challenges
findings.detail: The council set a balanced budget for 2026/27 without needing to drawdown reserves. However, 2025-26 saw significant underspends: £22.255m on General Fund capital and £16.036m on HRA capital. These large underspends may indicate difficulties in delivering planned capital projects or forecasting challenges.
findings.matters: Large capital underspends suggest the council is either over-planning or struggling to deliver projects on schedule. This affects the council's ability to invest in infrastructure and may indicate capacity issues.
findings.figures: Capital underspends: £22.255m General Fund; £16.036m HRA; 2025-26 General Fund revenue underspend £0.543m; HRA surplus £4.391m
findings.quote: The provisional outturn for 2025-26 was a £0.543m underspend on the General Fund revenue Account (subsequently contributing to reserves) and a surplus of £4.391m on the Housing Revenue Account (HRA)... the capital provisional outturn was a £22.255m underspend against the General Fund and £16.036m underspend against the HRA programmes

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement, 2025-26
findings.headline: Internal Audit Opinion is 'Reasonable Assurance' with one Limited Assurance audit in corporate governance (Transparency Act)
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit opinion for 2025-26 is Reasonable Assurance (not the highest level, which is Substantial). One audit received Limited Assurance in Corporate Governance related to Transparency Act. No 'No Assurance' audits were issued, but two audits received the highest Substantial Assurance level.
findings.matters: Reasonable (rather than Substantial) Assurance indicates the auditors have identified some control weaknesses. The Limited Assurance corporate governance audit compounds governance concerns.
findings.figures: 1 Limited Assurance audit; 2 Substantial Assurance audits; 8 Reasonable Assurance audits; 0 No Assurance audits
findings.quote: The Internal Audit Opinion for 2025/26 is Reasonable Assurance in relation to the framework of risk management, governance of the Council and internal control. In 2025/26 the HoIA has not reported any no Assurance opinion audits. One audit in relation to Corporate Governance (Transparency Act) was given a limited Assurance opinion

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement, 2025-26
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) in 2026-27 is 'very significant' and creates staffing and organizational change risks
findings.detail: Norfolk is part of devolution and local government reorganisation priority programme. For 2026-27, LGR is described as a 'very significant project.' Norwich is establishing a Programme Management Office, moving staff to Norfolk-wide workstreams, and managing internal workload. LGR uncertainty is cited as backdrop for continued reliance on interim and agency staff.
findings.matters: Major organizational restructuring creates uncertainty, distraction, and risk of losing institutional knowledge. The council's ability to manage current operations and debt may be affected during this transition.
findings.figures: LGR programme underway; Norwich Programme Management Office being set up
findings.quote: For 2026-27 LGR will be a very significant project. Work is underway to set up a Norwich Programme Management Office, to identify colleagues to move into Norfolk wide workstreams, to manage workload internally

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement, 2025-26
findings.headline: Performance sustainability at risk from external pressures including financial constraints and increased demand
findings.detail: While 77% of KPIs are on or above target, the council acknowledges that 'ongoing external pressures, including financial constraints, increased demand and wider system challenges, pose a risk to the sustainability of performance.' This weakness is noted alongside the need to review links between strategic priorities and resource allocation.
findings.matters: Acknowledged risk to performance sustainability due to financial constraints and increased demand signals that the council may struggle to maintain service levels. This is relevant to the council's ability to service debt.
findings.figures: 17 of 26 KPIs green (77%), 2 amber (9%), 3 red (14%)
findings.quote: Ongoing external pressures, including financial constraints, increased demand and wider system challenges, pose a risk to the sustainability of performance.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement, 2025-26
findings.headline: Information governance incidents and data protection issues including ICO complaints about FOI handling
findings.detail: 167 incidents referred for investigation in 2025-26 (133 confirmed as actual incidents). One ICO self-report made following contractor cyber attack affecting tenant data. Multiple FOI/EIR complaints to ICO discovered processing errors in the Civica system and email routing failures, resulting in at least one request not being received by the IG team. 57 FOI requests responded to after deadline.
findings.matters: Data breaches, ICO complaints, and processing failures in handling information requests indicate governance and security weaknesses. System failures in handling FOI requests suggest operational risks.
findings.figures: 167 incidents referred in 2025-26; 1 ICO self-report; 57 FOI requests late; 5 ICO complaints opened (4 awaiting decision)
findings.quote: In the financial year 2025-26, 167 instances were referred to the Information Governance Team for investigation. Of these, 34 were identified as not an incident... the Council has self-reported once to the ICO... 57 other requests were responded to after the deadline

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement, 2025-26
findings.headline: Transparency Code compliance audit identified limited assurance with 8 recommendations including 3 urgent
findings.detail: October 2025 external compliance audit on Local Government Transparency Code 2015 gave Limited Assurance opinion. Eight recommendations were made (3 urgent, 4 important, 1 routine). As of the statement date, 3 important recommendations remain outstanding, with implementation being tracked via Audit Tracker.
findings.matters: Limited assurance on transparency and governance compliance suggests weaknesses in how the council reports and operates. Outstanding urgent recommendations indicate issues not yet resolved.
findings.figures: 8 recommendations made; 3 urgent, 4 important, 1 routine; 3 important recommendations remain outstanding
findings.quote: In October 2025 an external audit was completed to establish the condition of our compliance of the Local Government Transparency Code 2015. The audit finding provided a limited assurance opinion. The audit made 8 recommendations: 3 as urgent, 4 as important and 1 as routine. Currently 3 of the recommendations remain as important.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement, 2025-26
findings.headline: NCSL company flagged for cashflow and financial performance issues requiring mitigation
findings.detail: The council's other significant company, NCSL, is noted as requiring mitigation due to financials and cashflow concerns. The position is marked as static with direction indicating issues remain to be managed through continued monitoring and Shareholder Panel oversight.
findings.matters: Cashflow and financial difficulties in council-owned companies can indicate problems with management, trading conditions, or the viability of the ventures, all of concern to lenders.
findings.figures: NCSL flagged as 'Requires Mitigation'; risk position static
findings.quote: NCSL financials and cashflow. Requires Mitigation

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement, 2025-26
findings.headline: Lion Homes subsidiary in Members' Voluntary Liquidation with process due to conclude June 2026
findings.detail: Lion Homes received Limited Assurance opinion in 2024-25. The council approved a Members' Voluntary Liquidation (MVL) in 2025 and the process is scheduled to conclude by June 2026. A temporary Company Secretary has been appointed to oversee this and support other council companies.
findings.matters: A subsidiary being liquidated indicates previous investments or ventures that did not succeed. This signals potential exposure to failed commercial activity that lenders need to understand.
findings.figures: MVL process due to conclude June 2026; temporary Company Secretary appointed
findings.quote: Lion Homes in 2024-25; MVL decision in 2025. MVL process dues to conclude June 2026

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement, 2025-26
findings.headline: External audit identified significant weaknesses in company governance and financial reporting controls
findings.detail: EY's Audit Results Report for 2024/25 flagged two Value for Money risks as significant weaknesses: arrangements for subsidiaries lacked effective governance, and financial reporting had insufficient audit evidence and resource issues. The council is responding by updating its constitution and working with auditors on closedown processes.
findings.matters: Audit weaknesses in financial reporting and company governance are red flags for lenders. They indicate the council may not have adequate controls over its finances and subsidiaries.
findings.figures: Two Value for Money risks identified as significant weaknesses in 2024/25 external audit
findings.quote: The Council should update its constitution to make provision for effective governance and management of any companies in which it has an interest, to provide comprehensive oversight of governance guidelines for all subsidiaries

findings.paper_title: Annex A -Council's 2026-2027 budget and medium term financial strategy - Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Car park income continues to underperform, requiring budget adjustment downward
findings.detail: The council identifies that achieving budgeted car park income continues to be a recurring challenge. The 2026-2027 budget is being adjusted downward to reflect this pattern, suggesting either demand weakness or pricing constraints.
findings.matters: A persistent income shortfall reduces discretionary resources and suggests pricing flexibility may be constrained by market or political factors
findings.figures: Car park income budgets adjusted downward for 2026-2027 (quantum not specified in excerpt)
findings.quote: Achieving budgeted levels of car park income remains a challenge and the 2026-2027 budgets will be adjusted to reflect this.

findings.paper_title: Annex A -Council's 2026-2027 budget and medium term financial strategy - Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation transition costs may fall on the council unfunded
findings.detail: Norwich is moving to a new unitary authority structure from April 2028, requiring one-off costs for ICT systems, workforce restructuring, harmonisation of pay and conditions, and redundancy or pension strain costs. The council has set aside £1m but explicitly states there is no guarantee the government will fund all costs.
findings.matters: An unfunded government reform creates contingent liability against reserves at a time when funding is tightening. The £1m provision may not cover actual costs, risking either service cuts or unplanned reserve depletion
findings.figures: £1,000,000 provision for LGR implementation; full cost undefined
findings.quote: At present, there is no guarantee that all such costs will be fully funded by government, creating a risk that Norwich may need to meet part of the transition costs from existing resources or reserves.

findings.paper_title: Annex A -Council's 2026-2027 budget and medium term financial strategy - Cabinet Report
findings.headline: £50m HRA PWLB loan due March 2026 with material refinancing cost risk
findings.detail: A £50m Housing Revenue Account PWLB loan matures in March 2026. The council notes that current interest rates (3.75%) are relatively high and would produce significantly higher debt costs if refinanced immediately. Current cash balances are sufficient to cover repayment, but refinancing decisions create a trade-off between immediate cost and cash position management.
findings.matters: A major refinancing timing decision affecting debt servicing costs. If rates remain high or the council cannot delay refinancing, HRA costs rise, potentially requiring rental increases beyond the 4.8% already proposed
findings.figures: £50,000,000 loan matures late March 2026; base rate currently 3.75%
findings.quote: cash balances are due to reduce significantly when a £50,000,000 PWLB Loan in respect of the HRA is repaid in late March 2026. Forecasts for interest rates show they will continue to stay relatively high over the Medium-Term resulting in a significantly higher interest rates if the loan is refinanced immediately.

findings.paper_title: Annex A -Council's 2026-2027 budget and medium term financial strategy - Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Business rates baseline reset will reduce Norwich's retained income by £1.67m
findings.detail: From April 2026, the government is implementing a full national reset of the Business Rates Retention System. Norwich's projected retained income falls to £6.6m in 2026-2027 from £8.27m in 2025-2026. The government describes this as redistributing historic growth retained since 2013. The reset coincides with a 2026 revaluation and new multipliers, adding uncertainty.
findings.matters: A permanent reduction in core funding narrows financial flexibility and increases reliance on council tax and reserves during a period of transition uncertainty
findings.figures: £6,600,000 retained income 2026-2027; reduction of £1,670,000 from 2025-2026
findings.quote: The projected retained income for Norwich is £6,600,000 in 2026-2027, a reduction of £1,670,000 from the 2025-2026 budgeted income.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Opinion Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Risk management not effective in key areas with known risks not mitigated in timely manner
findings.detail: The Internal Audit opinion notes that 'risk management arrangements are not as effective as they could be' specifically citing continued exposure in transparency compliance and DBS checks where 'known risks are not being mitigated in a timely manner.' The report states there is 'heightened risk that identified weaknesses continue to expose the Council to regulatory, reputational, and operational risks, due to delays in implementing mitigation actions.'
findings.matters: Delays in mitigating known risks suggest the council's risk management framework may not be driving appropriate prioritization or accountability for risk reduction
findings.figures: Overdue recommendations from transparency and DBS audits; delays in policy approval and dissemination
findings.quote: There is a heightened risk that identified weaknesses continue to expose the Council to regulatory, reputational, and operational risks, due to delays in implementing mitigation actions.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Opinion Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Internal controls inconsistent across council with specific weaknesses in data quality and process compliance
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit identifies strong controls in Housing Services but significant weaknesses elsewhere. Specific gaps are noted in transparency and publication controls with lack of ownership and absence of structured processes; data accessibility and quality with outdated, incomplete and non-compliant datasets; and DBS processes with gaps in data accuracy and oversight. The report concludes that 'internal control may not be sufficiently embedded across the Council currently, reducing overall assurance.'
findings.matters: Inconsistent controls across the council suggest systemic issues in control design or enforcement; data quality weaknesses can undermine financial reporting and decision-making
findings.figures: Weakness categories: transparency and publication controls; data accessibility and quality; DBS processes
findings.quote: Strong controls exist in specific service areas, but not across the Council; therefore, internal control may not be sufficiently embedded across the Council currently, reducing overall assurance.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Opinion Report 2025-26
findings.headline: 25 audit recommendations overdue at year-end, including three urgent, indicating slow implementation
findings.detail: As of March 2026, 25 recommendations from audits were past their due dates: 3 urgent, 12 important, and 10 routine. This includes urgent recommendations from the 2024/25 Transparency audit with revised completion dates pushed to May and June 2026, and an important Planning and Enforcement recommendation overdue since June 2025 now re-dated to June 2026. The report notes 'evidence of delayed or partial implementation, increasing the likelihood that risks remain active beyond acceptable tolerances.'
findings.matters: A large backlog of overdue actions suggests weak implementation governance and risk that control weaknesses remain unaddressed longer than acceptable tolerance levels
findings.figures: 25 recommendations past due date (3 urgent, 12 important, 10 routine); 5 closed post year-end but majority remain with revised dates
findings.quote: Evidence of delayed or partial implementation, increasing the likelihood that risks remain active beyond acceptable tolerances.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Opinion Report 2025-26
findings.headline: DBS checking process still carries safeguarding risk despite follow-up action
findings.detail: A follow-up audit of the 2024/25 DBS Checks audit found only one of five recommendations fully completed. Gaps persist in data accuracy, including two cases where DBS clearance dates were after employment start dates. No reporting to the Assurance Board occurred, and the new DBS policy and toolkit have not been formally approved or disseminated. The audit notes that risk remains in staff oversight and data quality, creating possibility of staff members in post without completed or renewed DBS checks.
findings.matters: Staff employed without proper DBS clearance represents a fundamental safeguarding failure and liability exposure for the council
findings.figures: 1 of 5 recommendations completed; 2 cases identified where DBS clearance was after employment start date; 4 new urgent recommendations raised
findings.quote: a level of risk still exists in oversight, processing and knowing your data which increases the possibility of staff members being in post without a DBS check being completed or renewed.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Opinion Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Transparency Code non-compliance with no clear ownership or oversight
findings.detail: The Corporate Governance (Transparency Act) audit gave a Limited opinion on the Council's compliance with the Local Government Transparency Code 2015. The audit identified a longstanding lack of senior management ownership, no clear internal policies defining roles and responsibilities, insufficient oversight including publication schedules or checklists, outdated and invalid links on the website, and significant gaps with most datasets missing publication criteria or unpublished. Eight recommendations were raised including three urgent; five remain open at year-end.
findings.matters: Non-compliance with statutory transparency requirements creates regulatory and reputational risk; the lack of ownership suggests weaknesses in governance structures and management accountability
findings.figures: 8 recommendations raised (3 urgent, 4 important, 1 routine); 5 still open at year-end
findings.quote: The audit revealed a longstanding lack of senior management ownership and accountability regarding the publication requirements of the Transparency Code 2015, with no clear internal policies defining roles and responsibilities.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Risk Register 2025-26 – Quarter 4
findings.headline: Three risks remain above risk appetite and cannot be fully eliminated (health and safety, cyber, business continuity)
findings.detail: CORP03 (H&S), CORP06 (business continuity) and CORP07 (cyber security) all have risk scores exceeding the council's risk appetite, and the council has determined these risks cannot be fully reduced. For cyber, the council notes that fully eliminating email-based attacks would require disabling email services entirely, which would critically impair service delivery. H&S compliance work continues but training and register completion has been slower than planned.
findings.matters: These are category risks the council has decided to tolerate rather than treat, indicating acceptance of inherent vulnerabilities in critical areas. A lender should understand that the council operates with elevated baseline risk in these domains and whether mitigation strategies are adequate.
findings.figures: CORP03: current 8, target 8, appetite 4; CORP06: current 16, target 16, appetite 4; CORP07: current and target exceed appetite 4; only 4 H&S procedures outstanding for completion by end May 2026
findings.quote: To fully reduce the risk in line with the risk appetite score would require controls that would place an operational burden on the council severely impacting service delivery. For example, while email is the most prevalent attack vector, eliminating this risk entirely would necessitate disabling or severely restricting email services.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Risk Register 2025-26 – Quarter 4
findings.headline: Workforce transition risks delayed by inability to staff the LGR programme management office
findings.detail: Multiple critical workforce actions for managing the LGR transition are marked RED (will not start until PMO is established) or AMBER (pending HR recruitment). These include developing workforce assurance arrangements, formalizing Norfolk-wide recruitment models, and deploying staff to backfill roles redeployed to transition work. The council has identified the need to manage leadership and decision-making capacity but these arrangements remain incomplete.
findings.matters: Effective LGR delivery depends on adequate staffing of governance and programme management. Delays in establishing transition structures could compress timelines, increase transition costs, and create service continuity risks if staff are not properly backfilled when deployed to LGR work.
findings.figures: Vesting date 1 April 2028 (23 months away); 20/80 external/internal resource split for LGR agreed; multiple RED-rated actions pending PMO establishment
findings.quote: Use staff resource identified in prioritisation exercise to backfill and review capacity impact including leadership and decision making - Red - Will be undertaken when PMO is established

findings.paper_title: Corporate Risk Register 2025-26 – Quarter 4
findings.headline: Business continuity infrastructure gaps, particularly power resilience and out-of-hours cover
findings.detail: CORP06 (business continuity) remains at risk score 16, well above the council's risk appetite of 4, with no improvement expected (target also 16). Specific gaps include reliance on old UK Power Network equipment and inadequate out-of-hours cover for some services. A power upgrade and rest centre were managed successfully in December 2025, but underlying infrastructure dependencies remain unresolved.
findings.matters: Business continuity failures could disrupt council operations and service delivery to residents. Infrastructure dependencies create concentration risk; the council has limited ability to mitigate power failures if they affect multiple services simultaneously.
findings.figures: Current risk score 16, target risk score 16, risk appetite 4; exercise programme planned for autumn 2026
findings.quote: Power resilience - reliance on old UK Power Network equipment and water egress through hatch

findings.paper_title: Corporate Risk Register 2025-26 – Quarter 4
findings.headline: New financial risk from Local Government Reorganisation and persistent budget pressures
findings.detail: Norwich has identified a new risk (CORP38A) that it may fail to budget for sufficient savings alongside LGR requirements and a challenging financial climate. The council notes it continues to operate in a high-risk environment driven by ongoing financial pressures despite receiving a provisional three-year financial settlement. The old general funding risk (CORP01) has been closed and folded into this more specific LGR financing risk.
findings.matters: The council is undergoing structural reorganisation with vesting on 1 April 2028, which creates significant budget and service delivery risks. A lender needs confidence that the council can maintain financial stability and achieve required savings during this major transition.
findings.figures: Risk score 12 (current and target), risk appetite 4; vesting date 1 April 2028; three-year financial settlement received; 50/50 funding split County/districts agreed
findings.quote: The Council continues to operate in a relatively high-risk environment, driven by ongoing financial pressures and a challenging wider economic context.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Review and Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: General fund financing costs jumped to 7.54% of net revenue, up from 0.97% budgeted estimate
findings.detail: The affordability ratio—the proportion of revenue consumed by debt financing—increased nearly eightfold between estimate and outturn. The council attributed this primarily to IFRS16 implementation and unbudgeted changes to minimum revenue provision, partially offset by higher investment income. The HRA ratio also increased from 33.70% to 37.44%, driven by capital costs written back to revenue.
findings.matters: A significant, unexpected increase in the financing cost burden reduces the council's financial flexibility and leaves less revenue available for service delivery or strategic priorities. Even if partly accounting-driven, this represents a material change in the council's actual financial position.
findings.figures: General fund 0.97% (estimate) vs 7.54% (actual); HRA 33.70% vs 37.44%
findings.quote: the general fund outturn is higher than the estimate mainly due to the implementation of IFRS16 and the unbudgeted changes to minimum revenue provision slightly offset by higher than expected budgeted investment income

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Review and Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital expenditure undershoot of £38.291m, representing 41% of final budget not spent
findings.detail: Actual capital spending was £56.477m against a final approved budget of £94.768m. The general fund underspent by £22.255m and the HRA by £16.036m. This substantial gap persisted despite budget revisions that included prior-year carry forwards, suggesting either reduced delivery capacity or delayed project progression.
findings.matters: Material underspending on planned capital programmes raises questions about the council's project delivery capability and the accuracy of its capital planning assumptions, both important factors in assessing whether the council can execute its financial and service strategies.
findings.figures: £38.291m total underspend; Final budget £94.768m vs actual £56.477m; GF variance £22.255m; HRA variance £16.036m
findings.quote: Actual capital spending was under budget for the year by £38.291m.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Review and Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Lion Homes subsidiary failed to repay £6.150m in loans and was approved for liquidation
findings.detail: Norwich's wholly-owned subsidiary Lion Homes Ltd did not repay any of the £6.150m in loans due on 31 March 2025. Cabinet approved a Members Voluntary Liquidation of the company on 9 July 2025, with completion expected in 2026-27. This represents a loss of asset value and questions the viability of the council's commercial subsidiary strategy.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's commercial ventures are sustainable and generating the returns necessary to service their debt. A subsidiary that cannot repay its obligations indicates asset value erosion and capital deployment risk.
findings.figures: £6.150m loans not repaid; liquidation completion 2026-27
findings.quote: During 2025-2026 LHL did not repay any of its loans which were due to be repaid on 31st March 2025. No new loans were made to LHL during 2025-26 and the total amount due to be repaid was £6.150m. On 9th July 2025 Cabinet approved the recommendation received from the Lion Homes Shareholder Panel to undertake a Members Voluntary Liquidation of the company.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement, 2024-25
findings.headline: Local government reorganisation scheduled for 2025-26 creates strategic uncertainty; affecting major capital decisions including company liquidation
findings.detail: Government announced in December 2024 plans for devolution and local government reorganisation in Norfolk, moving from two-tier to single-tier unitary councils. Norwich is one of six districts working to submit a three-council option in September 2025. This reorganisation was explicitly cited as a 'changed circumstance' that prompted the Lion Homes liquidation decision, indicating it is materially affecting the council's financial and strategic planning.
findings.matters: Pending reorganisation creates strategic uncertainty that constrains long-term capital and financing decisions. The council cannot plan beyond 2026 with confidence, and prior decisions (like company liquidation) are being made in the shadow of this change.
findings.figures: Three-council option to be submitted September 2025; local government reorganisation timetable confirmed
findings.quote: the confirmation of the local government reorganisation timetable and some relevant economic circumstances. As a consequence, further advice was commissioned to support the decision making about the future of the company

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement, 2024-25
findings.headline: City centre property acquired by the council has construction defects contrary to building regulations; full remediation costs not yet established
findings.detail: In late 2023, condition survey work identified that a city centre building recently acquired by the council had construction issues contrary to building regulations. Immediate deficiencies were addressed in early 2024 and regulatory authorities are content with medium-term state. However, the council is still establishing and costing the full programme of works to permanently rectify all issues. No figures for permanent remediation are disclosed.
findings.matters: A material capital asset has latent defects with unknown full remediation cost. This represents a contingent liability that may require future capital or revenue funding.
findings.figures: Costs for permanent rectification currently being established; immediate remediation undertaken early 2024
findings.quote: Further work is ongoing on establishing and costing the full programme of works to permanently rectify all issues with the building

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement, 2024-25
findings.headline: Internal audit found 'no assurance' on HR DBS (Disclosure and Barring Service) check processes, a statutory safeguarding requirement
findings.detail: An internal audit of business processes for DBS checks in 2024-25 resulted in a 'no assurance' finding. The matter was discussed by Audit Committee and remedial actions are underway as part of a wider action plan to raise standards in HR. This is a statutory safeguarding control: failure to properly check staff could expose the council and vulnerable adults to risk.
findings.matters: A 'no assurance' rating on a statutory compliance process (safeguarding) is a material control failure. It indicates the council may have appointed staff without proper vetting, creating legal and reputational exposure.
findings.figures: No assurance audit rating; corrective programme in progress, target May 2025
findings.quote: An internal audit of the business processes relating to the undertaking of DBS checks during 2024-2025 resulted in a no assurance finding

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement, 2024-25
findings.headline: The Halls operator procurement failed twice, with procedural inconsistencies and a challenge forcing abandonment; asset will now be run in-house
findings.detail: A 2024 tender for an external operator was withdrawn after procedural inconsistencies were identified in the invitation to tender and evaluation criteria. A second tender initiated in February 2025 was abandoned in September 2025 when a tenderer notified intent to challenge the outcome. The council has decided to maintain in-house operation. A lessons learnt review is underway. The Halls is a Grade 1 Listed building that received £3.6m of Town Deal capital funding.
findings.matters: Repeated procurement failures suggest internal governance weaknesses in procurement process management. Running a complex cultural asset in-house may not achieve intended commercial sustainability or value for money.
findings.figures: £3.6m Town Deal Capital funding secured in 2020; two procurement attempts in 2024-25
findings.quote: following an internal review, it was decided not to proceed with this procurement as procedural inconsistencies were identified in the invitation to tender and the evaluation criteria

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement, 2024-25
findings.headline: Nutrient Neutrality prevents planning applications for housing and constrains development income; credits supply remains insufficient
findings.detail: The council identified nutrient neutrality as a key weakness continuing to constrain development and income. The council joined Norfolk Environmental Credits Ltd joint venture for credit supply, but internal audit notes NEC currently has only small steady supplies and is unable to meet demand for large-scale development. This directly impacts planning fee income and the council's ability to deliver housing developments.
findings.matters: Development income and planning fees are material revenue sources; constraint on housing development is a structural income risk that affects financial planning and the council's ability to generate local growth.
findings.figures: Norfolk Environmental Credits supply described as 'small and steady'; unable to meet demand for large scale development
findings.quote: Nutrient Neutrality continues to constrain development and income; reliance on external credits supply

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement, 2024-25
findings.headline: Lion Homes subsidiary being wound up following governance concerns and deteriorating financial position
findings.detail: The council's wholly-owned housing company, where the council remains sole shareholder, received a 'Limited Assurance' audit opinion on governance. Following a business plan review and subsequent economic circumstances including local government reorganisation confirmation, Cabinet decided in July 2025 to complete a Members Voluntary Liquidation. Internal audit support is ongoing across company viability, whistleblowing, council and company oversight, and statement of accounts.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's exposure to company losses, any contingent liabilities, and the underlying governance and financial control failures that triggered liquidation.
findings.figures: Limited Assurance rating for Lion Homes governance; liquidation decision July 2025
findings.quote: further advice was commissioned to support the decision making about the future of the company, which was finally concluded by a Cabinet decision in July 2025 to complete a Members Voluntary Liquidation

findings.paper_title: Statement of Accounting Policies & State of External Audit
findings.headline: Subsidiary company Lion Homes owes £6.15m to the Council and is insolvent
findings.detail: Lion Homes (Norwich) Ltd could not repay its £6.15m outstanding loan to the Council as at 31 March 2025 and has entered liquidation. The council's accounts for this company are prepared on a break-up basis rather than going concern, indicating the loan is expected to be unrecoverable. This is explicitly stated as an exception to the going concern assumption applied to the rest of the council.
findings.matters: A £6.15m unrecoverable loan to a failed subsidiary represents material loss of council assets and signals weak governance over subsidiary investments. Lenders assess councils partly on the quality of their off-balance-sheet holdings and ability to manage corporate investments.
findings.figures: £6.15m outstanding loan; unable to repay as at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: The Statement of Accounts has been prepared on a 'going concern' basis except for Lion Homes (Norwich) Ltd. As at 31 March 2025 the company was unable to repay its outstanding £6.15m loan to the Council and has since entered into a member voluntary liquidation arrangement process.

findings.paper_title: Section 5 2026-2027 Treasury Management Strategy and Key Financial Indicators
findings.headline: Treasury advisor changed mid-year from MUFG to Arlingclose in November 2025
findings.detail: The council switched from MUFG Investor Services to Arlingclose as its treasury management advisor on 1 November 2025. This mid-year change occurred after the annual strategy had been set.
findings.matters: Mid-year advisor changes can signal dissatisfaction with previous advice or require recalibration of strategy, particularly around forecasts on interest rates.
findings.figures: Change effective 1 November 2025
findings.quote: The council used MUFG Investor Services as its external treasury management advisors until October 31st 2025. From 1st November 2025 the council appointed Arlingclose as its external treasury management advisors.

findings.paper_title: Section 5 2026-2027 Treasury Management Strategy and Key Financial Indicators
findings.headline: General Fund capital expenditure collapsing from £48m to £8m over three years
findings.detail: Capital expenditure plans for the General Fund drop sharply: £48.2m (2025-26) → £21.4m (2026-27) → £8.1m (2027-28). From 2028-29 onwards, the council plans to fund capital through revenue contributions of £21m-£25m annually, indicating shift away from capital investment.
findings.matters: A sharp reduction in capital investment signals either completion of major projects or financial constraint. Revenue contribution to capital is typically a sign of asset underinvestment.
findings.quote: Total General Fund Expenditure 48,171 / 22,353 / 8,060 with Revenue contribution 0 / 0 / 0 / 21,365 / 20,262 / 25,420

findings.paper_title: Section 5 2026-2027 Treasury Management Strategy and Key Financial Indicators
findings.headline: £150m of council debt maturing in three consecutive years with strategy to delay refinancing
findings.detail: Large tranches of PWLB debt mature: £53.2m in 2025-26, £57.5m in 2026-27, and £52.5m in 2027-28. The council's stated strategy is to 'wait as long as possible to refinance due to interest rates', betting on rates falling before these deadlines.
findings.matters: A council postponing refinancing of large debt tranches is exposed if rates don't fall as forecast, and creates lumpy near-term refinancing requirements.
findings.figures: £53.2m due 2025-26, £57.5m due 2026-27, £52.5m due 2027-28; total maturing debt £119.7m over three years
findings.quote: Current strategy is to wait as long as possible to refinance due to interest rates, so this may fall into 2027-2028.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Six internal control deficiencies identified, including one rated as high priority requiring immediate action.
findings.detail: A high-rated deficiency concerns debtor and creditor listings not meeting audit requirements, with unclear responsibility for data cleansing and multiple redirections when EY sought to identify owners. Five additional moderate-rated deficiencies were identified covering delays in HRA expense listings, PPE disclosure errors, NDR appeals provision errors, IFRS 16 disclosure defects, and revenue grant income recognition timing issues.
findings.matters: Control deficiencies of this number and severity indicate systemic weaknesses in financial processes. The high-rated item requires immediate remediation and suggests the finance function lacks clarity on responsibilities and system capabilities.
findings.figures: 1 high-rated, 5 moderate-rated control deficiencies
findings.quote: During our testing of Revenue Grants Received in Advance, we identified an instance where income had been recognised prior to the Council actually receiving the funds.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Management-imposed audit scope limitation: insufficient evidence for creditors and debtors.
findings.detail: During 2024/25, management prioritised work only on account balances where sufficient evidence could be obtained and acknowledged that adequate audit evidence could not be provided for creditors and debtors. These listings included significant opening and gross balances rather than the auditable format requested. Finance staff did not understand the Unit4 ERP system functionality to generate the required listings. This represents a deliberate limitation of the audit scope by management.
findings.matters: Inability to audit major balance sheet items (creditors and debtors) means the council cannot provide assurance on a significant portion of its current liabilities and receivables, key metrics for assessing financial health.
findings.figures: None specific amounts disclosed
findings.quote: During the 2024/25 audit, management prioritised work on account balances where sufficient evidence could be obtained and acknowledged that adequate audit evidence could not be provided for certain areas — specifically creditors and debtors.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Significant VFM weakness: inadequate financial reporting processes and systems.
findings.detail: The council does not have effective processes and systems to support statutory financial reporting. Key working papers were not provided in accordance with agreed timetables or suitable formats. Specifically, creditors and debtors working papers were incomplete, property valuations lacked sufficient supporting evidence, and the NDR appeals provision had errors due to a new team member's lack of familiarity with the process. Management acknowledges further work is required in these areas.
findings.matters: Weak financial reporting systems make it difficult for auditors to obtain necessary evidence and increase the risk of undetected errors in the financial statements. This undermines the reliability of the council's financial data.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: we have also identified a further weakness relating to the Council's arrangements for effective processes and systems to support statutory financial reporting requirements

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Significant VFM weakness: inadequate governance of subsidiaries and partnerships.
findings.detail: The council had no documented policies, procedures or governance oversight of its subsidiaries. The articles of association for Lion Homes did not require proper interaction with the council. Neither the Board of Directors nor the Shareholder Panel had terms of reference ensuring mandatory reporting to the council. The subsidiary operated independently with no requirement to report issues, resulting in financial problems not being identified in a timely manner and preventing effective intervention. This lack of structure significantly contributed to the challenges at the subsidiary.
findings.matters: Weak subsidiary governance put the council at financial risk and exposed taxpayers to uncontrolled company losses. It indicates the council cannot safely manage additional investments or companies.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: The Council did not have in place adequate policies, procedures or governance oversight of its part, or wholly, owned companies. This lack of oversight resulted in Council Members and Officers being unaware of inappropriate operating procedures and challenges at one of its subsidiaries.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Statutory deadline for publishing audited financial statements missed by nearly three months.
findings.detail: The financial statements were required to be published by 30 June 2025 under the Accounts and Audit Regulations, but were not published until 26 September 2025 (88 days late). This was due to delays in finalising group financial statements, largely stemming from the Lion Homes subsidiary issues. A Notice of Delay was issued. The audit itself cannot be finalised before the statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026 due to the deferred Audit Committee approval.
findings.matters: Missing statutory reporting deadlines indicates poor financial controls and is itself a regulatory breach. Delays in accounts publication delay audit completion and extend uncertainty about the council's true financial position.
findings.figures: Deadline 30 June 2025, actual publication 26 September 2025
findings.quote: The financial statements were not published by the 30 June 2025 deadline set out in the Accounts and Audit Regulations. This was due to delays in finalising the group financial statements. The required Notice of Delay was issued and the financial statements were subsequently published on 26 September 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Prior-period pension liability overstated by £35.1 million due to asset ceiling calculation error.
findings.detail: Management did not apply the required asset ceiling adjustment to the pension asset in 2023/24. The auditors identified that the defined benefit pension liability was overstated by £35.1 million. This material misstatement was not corrected in the 2024/25 financial statements per management's choice, meaning it remains in the accounts.
findings.matters: A £35.1m overstatement of pension liabilities materially misstates the council's financial position and net assets. This affects the balance sheet that lenders rely on for credit assessment.
findings.figures: £35.1 million
findings.quote: management obtained an updated asset ceiling report from the actuary highlighting that the defined pension liability is overstated by £35.1 million

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Wholly-owned housing subsidiary Lion Homes is entering member voluntary liquidation with uncertain loan recoverability.
findings.detail: The council has significant long-term debtor balances from loans to Lion Homes Ltd, now at risk of not being recoverable. Material errors were identified in the subsidiary's 2023/24 financial information, requiring a prior period adjustment in the 2024/25 statements. The council had no adequate governance arrangements to monitor the subsidiary, leaving members and officers unaware of operating problems until too late. The subsidiary operated independently with no mandatory reporting requirement to the council, preventing timely identification of financial issues.
findings.matters: Loss of a wholly-owned trading company represents a direct capital loss to the council. The loans may not be recovered. This reflects poor governance and exposes whether the council can safely operate subsidiary companies.
findings.figures: Long-term debtor balances from loans to subsidiary (amount not quantified in this section)
findings.quote: A financial sustainability risk has been identified concerning the council's wholly owned subsidiary, Lion Homes Ltd. The Council has significant long term debtor balances, arising from loans issued to the subsidiary. There is a risk that some of these balances may not be recoverable.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: 2024/25 financial statements will receive a disclaimed audit opinion, meaning the council's accounts cannot be relied upon.
findings.detail: The auditors cannot conclude that the 2024/25 financial statements are free from material and pervasive misstatement. This follows a disclaimed opinion in 2023/24. The auditors were unable to complete planned procedures for key audit areas including management override risks, capitalisation of expenditure, and property valuations. The lack of assurance over opening balances from the prior year disclaimer compounds the inability to assure current year movements and closing balances.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion means the council's financial statements cannot be relied upon for lending decisions or financial planning. This is the highest level of audit concern short of discovering fraud.
findings.figures: None specific, but covers all material account balances
findings.quote: We therefore anticipate issuing a disclaimed 2024/25 audit opinion.

findings.paper_title: Cover Report on the council's 2026-2027 budget and medium term financial strategy - Council
findings.headline: Finance director is in interim post rather than permanent appointment
findings.detail: The report is authored by 'Interim Director of finance (S151 Officer)' rather than a permanent appointment. This governance role is statutory and having it in interim status signals either a vacancy or transition.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if the council's chief finance officer post is stable; an interim S151 officer indicates staffing uncertainty that could affect financial continuity.
findings.figures: Report from: Interim Director of finance (S151)
findings.quote: Report from: Interim Director of finance (S151)

findings.paper_title: Cover Report on the council's 2026-2027 budget and medium term financial strategy - Council
findings.headline: Council maintains a budget risk reserve to cover financial risks in delivering 2026-2027 savings
findings.detail: Norwich has established a specific reserve 'to manage the financial risks associated with the delivery of the 2026-2027 budget savings', indicating uncertainty about whether planned savings will be fully realized.
findings.matters: A balanced budget that depends on savings that may not materialise is a risk; this reserve suggests the council itself is uncertain about delivery.
findings.figures: Reserve size not disclosed in this cover report.
findings.quote: The budget risk reserve to manage the financial risks associated with the delivery of the 2026-2027 budget savings.

findings.paper_title: Cover Report on the council's 2026-2027 budget and medium term financial strategy - Council
findings.headline: Financial risks to the council have increased due to wider economic environment
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that 'several financial risks to the council, some of which have increased' in response to economic changes. This suggests emerging pressures beyond the budget setting process itself.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know which new risks the council faces and whether the budget strategy adequately addresses them.
findings.figures: No quantification of these increased risks is provided.
findings.quote: Several financial risks to the council, some of which have increased, considering changes to the wider economic environment.

findings.paper_title: Cover Report on the council's 2026-2027 budget and medium term financial strategy - Council
findings.headline: Council has a reserve specifically established for risks from the liquidation of Lion Homes
findings.detail: Norwich maintains a 'companies reserve' to mitigate financial risks resulting from the liquidation of Lion Homes. This was the council's own housing company, and its failure has created ongoing financial liabilities that the council continues to manage.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand what exposure the council carries from failed subsidiaries and how much capital is tied up managing that risk.
findings.figures: Reserve size not disclosed in this cover report.
findings.quote: The companies reserve to mitigate financial risks resulting from the Liquidation of Lion Homes.

news_drafts.headline: Poundland and River Island subject to high court restructuring plans; Norwich unable to recover £320,587.04 in business rates debt
news_drafts.lead: Two significant commercial occupiers entering restructuring indicates commercial property market stress in Norwich and demonstrates credit risk concentration among major business ratepayers

news_drafts.headline: Council's audit recovery remains significantly behind expected timescale; 2025/26 opinion likely to be disclaimed, unqualified opinion unlikely before 2027/28
news_drafts.lead: Multi-year disclaimer opinions prevent reliable financial reporting. Lenders cannot assess the council's true financial health when financial statements lack audit assurance for multiple years.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix A - External Auditor’s Annual Report for Year ended 31 March 2025

news_drafts.headline: Non-compliance with laws and regulations not reported to auditors for seven months; council lacks formal whistleblowing logs and weak investigation processes
news_drafts.lead: Weak non-compliance procedures, slow reporting, and lack of whistleblowing mechanisms suggest governance and control environment deficiencies. Seven-month delays increase reputational and legal risk.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix A - External Auditor’s Annual Report for Year ended 31 March 2025
